name: Pedro Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in electrical engineering, so circuits, maths and a lab where half the equipment is older than me. I still live at home with my parents and my little sister, and I take the train in. Three nights a week I work the late shift at a petrol station, ten till six on weekends. I get home, sleep, go to a lecture, and repeat. My dad's an electrician, which is partly why I picked this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Every few years something is going to change the world, and mostly it changes a few spreadsheets. At the petrol station we've had self-pay screens for years and I still stand there at 3am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my course stays worth doing, and Dad's trade stays safe too. I'd still have to get through the maths, which I find hard, and my grades are only average. The worry is the cost, not the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. Same shifts, same degree, same train. If I could, I'd ask Dad if I could shadow him on a few jobs in the holidays, so I get hands-on hours and some pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Tired but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the worry is the cost. What costs are you facing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan covers fees, but I have to cover train tickets, books and a laptop. I put 60 a month aside, and some months it's nothing. If my petrol shifts got cut, I'd be in trouble quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do your parents help with money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They keep the roof and the food on the table, and that's it. Mum works in a school kitchen and her hours aren't guaranteed. I don't ask for more.

say: Every few years something is meant to **change the world**, and mostly it changes a few spreadsheets.
The self-pay screens haven't removed me from the **petrol station**.
think: My course stays **worth doing** and Dad's trade stays safe too.
The worry is **cost**, with average grades and thin savings.
do: **Carry on** with the same shifts, the same degree and the same train.
**Shadow** Dad on electrical jobs in the holidays for pay and hands-on hours.
feel: **Tired** but okay, because nothing new is landing on me.
S0.quote: I put 60 a month aside, and some months it's nothing.
fieldNote: His **worry** is money, not technology, which keeps a quiet world uneasy.
His dad's trade is a **safety net** he can lean on without asking for cash.
Distrust of **hype** comes from what he sees at the petrol station.

steps.text: Keep the petrol station night shifts through the year
Shadow Dad on electrical jobs in the holidays
Put 60 a month aside, even if it's less

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be overblown at first and then it will bite. It will take over a lot of the screen work, the kind of thing office people do all day. I'd tell my mates doing business and computing to watch out, because they're closer to it than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my field is less exposed, because wiring and power systems need people on site. But design work and checking might go to software, which means fewer junior engineering jobs. I'm not good with new software, and I know that's a weak spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick to the hands-on side. I'd ask for extra lab time, push for a placement at a utility or an installer, and work on my weakest tools, like the simulation software I avoid. I'd also keep the night job, because the money matters more than anything fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, honestly. Not scared, just aware that I'm not the quick one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you avoid some software. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like to understand a thing before I use it. When something is new, I wait until it's proven. But I know that can put me behind the people who dive in and figure it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you ask for help with the software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lab partner Tomas, who's good at it, and my dad's apprentice. I'd rather learn from a person than from an AI chat.

say: It will be **overblown** at first and then it will bite.
My mates in **business and computing** are closer to it than I am.
think: Wiring and power systems need **people on site**, so my field is less exposed.
Design checking could go to software, meaning fewer **junior** jobs.
do: Push for a **placement** with a utility or an electrical installer.
Practise the **simulation software** I avoid, with help from a lab partner.
feel: **Uneasy** and aware that I'm not the quick one.
S1.quote: When something is new, I wait until it's proven. But I know that can put me behind the people who dive in and figure it out.
fieldNote: He knows his **resistance** to new tools is a real weak spot.
He leans on **people** rather than software for learning.
His field is **hands-on**, which helps, but junior design roles still look thinner.

steps.text: Apply for a placement at an electrical installer
Practise the simulation software with my lab partner
Keep the night job for steady money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and nobody is prepared. I'd say something like, let's wait and see what is real before we panic, but I'd mean I'm worried. Governments don't move this quickly, so I wouldn't count on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be rattled. By 2028 I'd be in second year, and everything in the thinking side of engineering could be done by machines. My dad's work with his hands would last longer, until about 2031 or later, and I'd probably follow him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think seriously about quitting the degree and getting an electrician's apprenticeship through my dad's contacts. That's paid, practical, and the loan stops growing. I'd stay on the night shifts to keep money coming and try not to spend a penny I don't need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stressed. Mostly about money and about disappointing my parents, who were proud I got in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say if you left the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would be sad at first, then practical. Dad would be quietly pleased, I think, because he thinks trades are safer. But he wouldn't say it. They'd both worry about the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I could see a clear sign that engineers who understand physical systems are still wanted. If a firm told me, we'll hire you in three years, I'd stay. Without that, apprentice it is.

say: It's **too fast**, and nobody is prepared.
Governments don't move this quickly, so I wouldn't **count** on them.
think: By 2028 the **thinking side** of engineering could be done by machines.
My dad's **hand work** would last longer, and I'd probably follow him.
do: Look at an **electrician's apprenticeship** through Dad's contacts.
Keep the **night shifts** and not spend a penny I don't need to.
feel: **Stressed** about money and about disappointing my parents.
S2.quote: If a firm told me, we'll hire you in three years, I'd stay. Without that, apprentice it is.
fieldNote: The **fallback** is concrete and close to home: his dad's trade.
He fears **disappointing** his parents as much as the loan.
He doesn't count on **government**, which fits a pragmatic and sceptical centre view.

steps.text: Ask Dad about an electrician apprenticeship place
Keep the night shifts and track every pound
Ask the faculty for a written plan on engineering jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare and short enough that you shouldn't sit on your hands. I'd tell younger kids at my old school to check what they're picking. I wouldn't be dramatic about it, but I'd take it seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel better than in the 2028 case. I'd finish my degree in 2029, so I'd graduate into AGI. The hands-on work follows around 2034, which would give me some years if I stay on the practical side. I'd pick power and installation over design.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, and in the holidays I'd work with Dad to get my practical hours and a licence. I'd learn the software I avoid, slowly, a bit each term. I'd also save a bit more from the petrol station and look for a placement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Concerned but steady. There's a way through it, and it involves work, not luck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the software slowly. What changes your mind about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time. With five years I can try it without being under pressure. I won't be first, but I'll know enough not to be left behind. A bit each term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the degree started feeling pointless in third year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish anyway, because I'd have paid for it. A degree plus Dad's licence would look better than either one alone.

say: Five years is long enough to prepare and short enough that nobody should **sit still**.
I'd tell younger kids to check what they're **picking**.
think: I'd graduate **into** AGI in 2029, which is a risk.
Hands-on work lasts until about **2034**, so I'd pick power and installation.
do: **Work** with Dad in the holidays to get practical hours and a licence.
Learn the **software** I avoid, a bit each term.
feel: **Concerned** but steady, since there's a way through that involves work, not luck.
S3.quote: A degree plus Dad's licence would look better than either one alone.
fieldNote: He plans to **combine** the degree with his dad's trade rather than choose one.
**Time** is what makes him willing to try the software.
He frames the answer around **work, not luck**, typical of his steady, practical outlook.

steps.text: Work holidays with Dad toward electrician hours and a licence
Learn one new simulation tool each term
Save extra from petrol station shifts each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to deal with it, and I'd tell people to stay level-headed. I'd say the trades and a degree together make a good plan. I wouldn't rush to change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel fairly okay. By 2036 I'd be 28, I'd have a qualification and some site experience. Robots come about 2039, so I'd have a decent run before that. The thinking jobs are the first to change, but I'd be partly on the practical side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and take a graduate job at an energy firm or an installer. I'd build up savings to get my own place. I'd try the AI tools at work once they're proven and the others are using them. No rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. It would be a long road, but not a frightening one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your biggest worry in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Debt and slow wages. If the jobs are fewer and the pay is flat, ten years of paying back a loan is a long time. I'd like to know that the degree really helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it compare with the 2031 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About the same plan, but with time to breathe. In the five-year one, I'd feel a bit hurried. With ten I can go at my own speed, and that suits me.

say: Ten years is enough, so **stay level-headed**.
A trade and a degree together make a **good plan**, and I wouldn't rush to change anything.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28 with a **qualification** and site experience.
Robots come around **2039**, so I'd have a decent run first.
do: **Finish** the degree and take a graduate job at an energy firm or installer.
**Save** toward my own place and try AI tools at work once proven.
feel: Mostly **settled**, on a long road that isn't frightening.
S4.quote: If the jobs are fewer and the pay is flat, ten years of paying back a loan is a long time.
fieldNote: His remaining worry is **debt and slow pay**, not machines.
He prefers to go at his **own speed**, which a decade allows.
The decision to try AI tools remains **conditional** on others using them first.

steps.text: Take a graduate job at an energy firm or installer
Save toward renting a place of my own
Try AI tools at work once colleagues use them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time and I'm still paying for the degree. What would help is real support for people who lose their route, like paid apprenticeships, and honest talk from the university about what jobs will exist.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I'd blame. Nobody, really, because most of the noise about this is from people selling something. I just want to know what's real before I decide, and I'd like one honest person to tell me.

headlineQuote: Most of the noise about this is from people selling something. I just want to know what's real before I decide, and I'd like one honest person to tell me.
portrait: Pedro is 18, studies **electrical engineering** and still lives at home, working night shifts at a petrol station.
He is a centrist with little patience for **hype**, and he avoids new software until it's proven.
His dad's trade is a **fallback** and a plan: a degree plus an electrician's licence.
Thin money makes him **uneasy** in quiet worlds, and alarmed if AGI arrives by 2028.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most, since he'd still be paying for the degree.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **apprenticeships** for people who lose their route.
Honest advice from the university about which **jobs** will exist.
